text: processes” Prepared for the U.S. Department of Energy ARDAP program in talks with the Department of Defense on workforce efforts designed in part to address the critical need for training of engineers and trades people to design and manufacture electron beam welding processes. The design team and fabrication team both need expertise in specifics of working with electron beam welding. The physics and materials science of how this process functions is drastically different from traditional arc welding processes, and as such subject-specific training is needed. Without this training, the team involved will at best be operating inefficiently, at worst ineffectively, and will have major issues with scaling production or accommodating prototype part development. EH&S The major safety concerns related to electron beam welding include high voltage electricity, heavy equipment and robotics, vacuum environment, and x-rays. Training on the dangers of each of these factors is required for safe design with and operation of the EBW equipment. The vacuum chamber is designed to contain the x-rays and the electron beam gun does not operate with the chamber open so this reduces potential safety concerns. Heavy equipment and robotics safety training are no different than standard trainings; the main variation of these systems from standard robotic or motions systems is the requirement that they are effectively shielded so that the EMF does not interfere with the beam, and that they are designed to operate in the convective cooling absent vacuum environment. High voltage electricity has particular dangers than need specific training to understand so that safe operation can be achieved. Maintenance and OEM Support The basic function of an electron beam welding system is similar to a scanning electron microscope (SEM). The complex electromagnetic systems that make up the beam column require highly specific training to maintain and repair. A major difference between EBW and SEM is that and EBW system have much higher power and also generate vapor. The associated power management system for EBW requires additional subject matter expertise to maintain and repair. The vacuum system is another technology that requires highly specific technical expertise for maintenance and repair. In addition to these core components of the EBW system, the CNC controls, sensors, and motion control systems all require advanced training to ensure effective maintenance and repair. Due to the very broad technical expertise required to maintain and repair this equipment, rapid EBW OEM support is critical. When comparing EBW technologies world leaders include the Pro-Beam Group, Sciaky Inc., and the Global Beam Technologies Group (GBT) which owns both the US company PTR, and the German company Steigerwald Strahltechnik GmbH. All of these companies have major customer positions in the USA working across industry, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Energy. Support is particularly important in the case of a catastrophic failure where diagnostics and replacement components are needed immediately, and any delay would lead to loss of business and potential bankruptcy.
